scams.name: Old Town Scottsdale 'Skin' & Venmo-PIN Scam
scams.description: Old Town Scottsdale has a documented "skin" scam, active since 2024 and 2025, in which a stranger approaches and asks to borrow your phone to call a ride. If your Venmo account has no PIN protection, the thief quickly sends himself $500 to $3,000 before handing the phone back. The scam continued in 2025 through golf-cart drivers operating tourist transport. In this variant, cart drivers offer tourists "free rides" and then extract Venmo or Zelle payments during the ride. The defensive playbook: (1) never hand an unlocked phone to a stranger for any reason; (2) enable PIN protection on Venmo, Zelle, Cash App, and all payment apps; (3) decline all "free" cart rides from strangers in Old Town Scottsdale; (4) if a stranger genuinely needs to call for help, offer to make the call yourself on your phone with the speaker on; (5) Scottsdale has posted fraud warnings in tourist areas, so take them seriously.
scams.avoidance: Never hand an unlocked phone to a stranger; make the call yourself on speaker. Enable PIN protection on Venmo, Zelle, Cash App, PayPal, and all payment apps. Decline "free" cart rides from strangers in Old Town Scottsdale. If someone genuinely needs help, call 911 on their behalf. Report any attempt to Scottsdale PD (480-312-5000).
scams.location: Old Town Scottsdale pedestrian area, bar strip near Marshall Way, Scottsdale Waterfront, nightlife venues around Camelback
scams.tldr: In Old Town Scottsdale, a stranger asks to borrow your phone to call a ride, then sends himself $500 to $3,000 through your unprotected Venmo before returning it. A 2025 variant uses golf-cart drivers who offer "free rides" and extract payments along the way.

scams.name: Phoenix Sky Harbor (PHX) Rideshare & Taxi Scams
scams.description: From Phoenix Sky Harbor (PHX), a legitimate rideshare (Uber or Lyft) to central Phoenix runs $18 to $35 depending on surge pricing; a licensed taxi runs $30 to $45 on the meter; and the Valley Metro light rail from the 44th Street/Washington station is $2 per ride to downtown. The scam variants are: (1) drivers soliciting at baggage claim who offer a "flat $60" to downtown or Scottsdale; (2) "limo" touts quoting $100 or more for standard trips; (3) drivers insisting on a cash "tip" or "airport surcharge" beyond the app total at drop-off. The PHX SkyTrain connects to the 44th Street light rail station for free and is scam-proof. For older travelers arriving at PHX, the playbook is: (1) take the free PHX SkyTrain from the terminal to 44th Street/Washington, then the Valley Metro light rail to downtown ($2); (2) catch an Uber or Lyft at the official rideshare pickup zone (the designated curb at Terminal 3 or 4); (3) take a licensed taxi with the meter running for $30 to $45 to downtown; (4) never engage drivers soliciting at baggage claim; (5) for Scottsdale trips, take an Uber or Lyft for $25 to $40 and avoid "limo" touts quoting $100 or more.
scams.avoidance: Take the free PHX SkyTrain to 44th Street/Washington, then the Valley Metro light rail to downtown ($2). Use Uber or Lyft at the designated pickup zone and screenshot the fare estimate before boarding. A licensed taxi with the meter running is $30 to $45 to downtown. Avoid drivers soliciting at baggage claim.
scams.location: Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) terminals 3, 4; 24th Street light rail station; official rideshare pickup zones
scams.tldr: At Phoenix Sky Harbor, drivers soliciting at baggage claim push "flat $60" fares and limo touts quote $100-plus when a metered taxi runs $30 to $45 and the light rail costs $2. Take the free SkyTrain to the light rail or use the official rideshare curb.

scams.name: Grand Canyon Day-Trip Tour Package Overcharge
scams.description: The Grand Canyon South Rim is a 3.5-hour drive from Phoenix (230 miles). Legitimate Grand Canyon day-trip operators booked through Viator, GetYourGuide, or Detours American West charge $150 to $250 per person for a full-day bus tour with the entry fee included. Hotel-concierge packages mark this up 30 to 80 percent, charging $300 to $450 per person for the same experience. The scam variants are: (1) hotel concierge "exclusive" Grand Canyon tours at $300 or more; (2) online third-party resellers who disappear after payment; (3) "helicopter tour" packages at $500 or more when Grand Canyon helicopter operators such as Maverick and Papillon charge $250 to $400 booked direct; (4) "Antelope Canyon plus Grand Canyon" combo tours at $600 or more per person. For older travelers, the clean route is: (1) book through Viator, GetYourGuide, or Tiqets for a $150 to $250 bus tour; (2) for a helicopter, book direct with Maverick Helicopters or Papillon at $250 to $400; (3) note that Grand Canyon National Park entry is $35 per vehicle (a 7-day pass) if you self-drive; (4) for multi-stop Antelope Canyon plus Grand Canyon tours, expect $350 to $450 booked direct, not $600 or more; (5) avoid hotel-concierge packages at $300 or more per person.
scams.avoidance: Book through Viator, GetYourGuide, or Detours American West for $150 to $250. For a helicopter, book Maverick Helicopters or Papillon direct ($250 to $400). To self-drive, rent a car plus pay the $35 park entry for a 7-day pass. An Antelope Canyon plus Grand Canyon combo should be $350 to $450 direct, not $600 or more. Pay with a credit card for chargeback leverage.
scams.location: Phoenix hotel concierges, Scottsdale tour-desk booth operators, third-party online Grand Canyon tour sellers
scams.tldr: A Grand Canyon day trip from Phoenix costs $150 to $250 per person booked direct through Viator or GetYourGuide, but hotel concierges and tour-desk booths mark the same trip up 30 to 80 percent to $300 to $450, and combo tours can hit $600 or more.

scams.name: Scottsdale & Phoenix Timeshare Presentation Hustle
scams.description: Scottsdale and Phoenix are major timeshare-sales hubs, with resort operators offering "free" gifts (a round of golf, a spa treatment, a $100 dinner voucher) in exchange for a 90-minute "presentation." The presentation actually runs 2 to 4 hours, using high-pressure tactics to push timeshare purchases of $15,000 to $50,000. The scam variants are: (1) a mall or tourist-strip tout who offers a "free Phoenix tour" that turns out to be a timeshare pitch; (2) a "Vacation Club" membership at $10,000 to $30,000 with opaque annual fees; (3) "exit" companies that charge $5,000 to $15,000 to help victims cancel existing timeshares, many of which are themselves scams. For older travelers in Scottsdale and Phoenix, the defensive posture is: (1) never accept "free gift" offers that require attending a "presentation" — the time cost and high-pressure sales make it a net negative even with the free gifts; (2) if you do attend, bring a printed copy of the rule "I will not sign anything today" and stick to it; (3) Arizona allows a 7-day right of rescission for timeshare contracts, so cancel within 7 days if you signed under pressure; (4) for genuine rescission assistance, use the state attorney general's office (azag.gov), not "exit" companies.
scams.avoidance: Never accept "free gift" offers that require attending a presentation. If you attend, bring the rule "I will not sign anything today" and stick to it. Use Arizona's 7-day right of rescission if you signed under pressure. Report to the Arizona AG Consumer Protection office (azag.gov). Avoid "exit" companies charging $5,000 or more; use the state AG instead.
scams.location: Old Town Scottsdale timeshare sales centers, Scottsdale Waterfront resorts, Phoenix-area Marriott Vacation Club venues
scams.tldr: Scottsdale and Phoenix resorts offer free golf, spa treatments, or dinner vouchers for a "90-minute" timeshare pitch that runs 2 to 4 hours and pressures you toward a $15,000 to $50,000 purchase. Decline, and use Arizona's 7-day rescission if you signed.

scams.name: Scottsdale & Desert Resort Dining Gratuity Surprise
scams.description: Many Scottsdale resort restaurants and Phoenix tourist venues automatically add an 18 to 22 percent gratuity to parties of 6 or fewer, going beyond the standard "groups of 8 or more" convention. Some add a "service charge" that is not gratuity, so the server still needs a tip on top of it. Menu disclosure varies wildly. The scam variants are: (1) a "20% auto-gratuity" added to a 2-person dinner; (2) a "3% service charge" that sounds small but is separate from the tip; (3) a "resort fee" of $25 to $50 added to the room bill without clear disclosure; (4) a "health and wellness fee," a post-COVID holdover in some venues. For older travelers dining in Scottsdale and Phoenix, the practical rules are: (1) check the bill for "gratuity" or "service charge" lines before adding a tip, to avoid double-tipping; (2) ask the server directly, "Is gratuity included?" before signing; (3) remember that a "service charge" is not the same as gratuity, so ask who receives it; (4) confirm any resort fee with the hotel at check-in; (5) if a restaurant adds an auto-gratuity for a party of 2 to 4 without disclosure, raise it politely before paying or ask for a manager.
scams.avoidance: Check the bill for "gratuity" or "service charge" lines before adding a tip. Ask the server directly, "Is gratuity included?" Confirm any resort fee at hotel check-in. If an auto-gratuity is added without disclosure for a party of 2 to 4, request a manager review. Keep a photo of the menu pricing before ordering to verify the final bill.
scams.location: Scottsdale resort restaurants, Phoenix tourist-area venues, Waterfront dining, Camelback Corridor restaurants
scams.tldr: Scottsdale resorts and Phoenix venues often add an 18 to 22 percent auto-gratuity to small parties, plus separate "service charges" and "resort fees" that aren't tips. Check the bill for these lines before tipping again, and ask the server whether gratuity is included.

scams.name: Phoenix Rental Car 'Damage' & Insurance Upsell Scams
scams.description: Phoenix is a major rental-car market, drawing snowbirds, spring-training fans, and Grand Canyon self-drive trips. Rental operators at the PHX airport Rental Car Center include Hertz, Enterprise, Avis, Budget, Alamo, Thrifty, Fox, Dollar, and Payless. The scam variants are: (1) counter-agent pressure to accept "zero-excess" insurance at 2 to 3 times what credit card coverage already provides; (2) post-return "damage claims" for pre-existing or fabricated scratches, often raised weeks after you return the car; (3) a fuel-policy "return full" dispute in which the claimed level is 0.1 gallon less than what you filled; (4) toll-system "convenience fee" charges for bypassing SunPass — a $15 "administrative fee" per toll, plus the toll itself. For older travelers renting at PHX, the protective playbook is: (1) avoid Fox, Payless, and Sixt (budget aggregators with the highest complaint rates in Phoenix), and use Hertz, Enterprise, or Alamo for major rentals; (2) at pickup, take a video walk-around narrating every visible scratch and the tire condition; (3) photograph all four sides, the roof, the wheels, and the undercarriage with your phone camera; (4) decline "zero-excess" insurance if your credit card provides rental coverage (Chase Sapphire, Amex Platinum, and most Visa Signature cards do); (5) for tolls, pre-arrange SunPass at the counter or pay cash at the toll plazas, and never use the "automatic toll plan," which adds $15 per toll; (6) return the car with the same fuel level you picked up; (7) dispute any post-return damage claim with your credit card within 48 hours using your photo and video evidence.
scams.avoidance: Avoid Fox, Payless, and Sixt at PHX; use Hertz, Enterprise, or Alamo. Take a video walk-around at pickup, narrating every scratch and the tire condition. Decline "zero-excess" insurance if your credit card provides rental coverage. Pre-arrange SunPass at the counter or pay tolls in cash, and skip the "automatic toll plan." Dispute post-return damage claims with your credit card within 48 hours using your photo and video evidence.
scams.location: PHX airport rental car center, Phoenix city-center rental offices, Scottsdale resort partnered rental operators
scams.tldr: At the PHX Rental Car Center, agents push "zero-excess" insurance at 2 to 3 times credit card coverage, file weeks-later "damage" claims for fabricated scratches, and add $15-per-toll "convenience fees." Film a walk-around at pickup and decline coverage you already have.
